summary:
LavaTwin is an open-data workflow that screens Earth terrain for analogs of lava-tube sites proposed for Moon and Mars bases. 
Using NASADEM (Earth), LRO LOLA (Moon) and the NASA-ESA MOLA/HRSC blended model (Mars), we resampled all maps to about 200 m and computed slope and roughness. We compared 20 x 20 km patches at Marius Hills (Moon) and an Arsia Mons lava flow (Mars) with 646 sliding windows over Vietnam's Krong No volcanic field and with windows over a non-volcanic control, the Mekong Delta, using the normalized Wasserstein distance (0 = identical). 
Moon: the best Krong No window (lowland, about 220 m elevation) scores 0.066 versus 0.471 for the best control window, but median windows are similar (0.861 versus 0.919), so only part of the region matches. 
Mars: no Krong No window matches closely (best 0.628 versus 0.284 for the control), so the hypothesis is not supported for this site. Terrain similarity is not geological similarity, so matches must be checked against basalt geology maps, and only one site per body was tested at about 200 m resolution. 
Lava tubes may shelter future bases, and nearby analogs could let teams rehearse rover routes and lava-tube surveys at lower cost before real missions. The workflow is reproducible on free data and can be rerun for any region or site.
details:
LavaTwin is an open-data workflow that looks for places on Earth whose terrain resembles lava-tube sites proposed for Moon and Mars bases. It converts NASA and ESA elevation models of Marius Hills (Moon), an Arsia Mons lava flow (Mars), the Krong No volcanic field (Vietnam) and a non-volcanic control (Mekong Delta) into a common frame, resamples them to about 200 m, and computes slope and local roughness. A 20 x 20 km patch at each Moon/Mars site is compared with every 20 x 20 km window (5 km stride) across Krong No and across the control, using the normalized Wasserstein distance between slope and roughness distributions (0 = identical). The output is a ranked similarity map plus a summary of the best and median windows per region.

For the Moon, the best Krong No window scores 0.066 against Marius Hills, versus 0.471 for the best control window, so part of Krong No is a candidate analog. The median windows are similar (0.861 versus 0.919), so only some Krong No terrain matches. For Mars, no Krong No window matches the Arsia Mons flow well (best 0.628), and the flat Mekong Delta scores better (0.284). We report this negative result openly.

The method is low-cost, reproducible and built entirely on free, open data. It can be rerun for any region and any Moon/Mars site, and it ranks places by measurable terrain properties instead of intuition.

Lava tubes may shelter future bases. Finding nearby Earth terrain with similar slope and roughness could let teams rehearse rover routes and lava-tube surveys closer to home and at lower cost before real missions. The results are meant as a screening step that tells geologists where to look first, not as proof that a site is a true analog.

Python in Google Colab (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib), GitHub for the code and README, Google Earth/Maps for checking coordinates. Data: NASADEM (NASA Earthdata, LP DAAC), LRO LOLA gridded DEM (NASA PDS), and the MGS MOLA / MEX HRSC blended Mars DEM (USGS Astrogeology), plus Cushing (2012) for Mars lava-tube candidate locations. No special hardware was needed. An AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) was used for presentation-making and interpretating results.

We use a volcanic field in Vietnam as a candidate analog and test it against both the Moon and Mars with a like-for-like window scan and a non-volcanic control. We report the best and the median window so one lucky window cannot drive the conclusion, and we include a negative result instead of only the favorable one.

Different map projections, units and longitude conventions across Earth, Moon and Mars; matching resolution (about 200 m) and window size (20 x 20 km) so the comparison is fair; the selection effect of picking a "best" window; the choice of control region; and the fact that terrain similarity is not geological similarity, so matches still need checking against basalt geology maps. We also noted differences in gravity, climate and lava-tube size, the limited resolution (individual pits and cones are not resolved), and that only one site per body was analyzed.

Finally, thank you to the NASA Space Apps Challenge organizers, to NASA, ESA, USGS and the LRO, MOLA and HRSC teams for their free and open data, and to the judges for reviewing our work.
